Buildathon 2026 Participant Guide

This is your operating guide for the Bengaluru Tech Week Buildathon. Read it before arrival, keep it open during the build, and use the final checklist before you submit. The submission deadline is 3:00 PM IST.
Your day
Time
What happens
What you should do
8:00–9:00
Breakfast, check-in and setup
Arrive early. Confirm your team, laptop, power, GitHub access, development tools and optional Databricks Free Edition access.
9:00–12:00
Kickoff and build session
Choose one Entire track, fork only after the official start, configure the required Entire workflow, build a narrow end-to-end slice and create your early checkpoints.
12:00–1:00
The Noon Curveball and lunch
Stop, preserve your last stable version, close the current agent session, receive the new constraint, start fresh and reconstruct the project from checkpoint context before editing.
1:00–3:00
Build session and submission
Implement the constraint, test the changed behavior, verify the Entire Graph evidence, create the final checkpoint, finish BUILDATHON.md and submit before 3:00 PM.
3:00–5:00
Judging and winner announcement
Keep the project runnable. Mentors complete first-level review; eight finalists present; judges deliberate and awards are announced.


What makes this Buildathon different
You are not being asked to produce a generic app around a prompt. You must build a useful developer product on one of three Entire open-source surfaces, preserve decision context through checkpoints, use structural evidence from the Entire Graph where required, and respond to an additional non-negotiable constraint revealed at noon.
Teams may also make Databricks essential to the same product and opt in to the separate Best Use of Databricks awards. There remains one project and one submission; a team may win both an Entire main-challenge prize and a Databricks award.
Before you arrive
Bring and verify
A laptop, charger and any adapters you need. Bring a power bank only as a backup; do not rely on it for the full day.
A working GitHub account with permission to create forks and push to your fork.
Your preferred coding agent and local development tools already installed and signed in.
A local runtime that can run tests and a browser or API client that can demonstrate the product.
A Databricks Free Edition account if your team wants to compete for Best Use of Databricks. Create and open it before the event so account issues do not consume your build window.
A fallback demo asset: a recent screenshot or short screen recording for any step that depends on a live service.
Allowed before 9:00 AM
Research, user discovery, problem framing, sketches and planning are allowed before the official start. Implementation must begin after 9:00 AM on 6 September. Do not arrive with a prebuilt solution, completed feature branch or reusable implementation that gives your team an unfair head start.
Team readiness
Name one person as submission owner. This person checks every link and submits before 3:00 PM.
Name one person as the final demo owner. They should be able to explain the system even if another teammate wrote most of the code.
If using Databricks, choose one final demo workspace and one deployment owner. Use Git for shared code; never store secrets in the repository.
Agree how you will record decisions, failures and verified outcomes in checkpoints and BUILDATHON.md.
Account links
Create or open Databricks Free Edition
Buildathon details and updates
Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct







Choose one Entire innovation track
Your team must select one track. The project should solve a real developer or agent-workflow problem and make Entire essential to the solution. Adding Entire only for tracking, without using its context, checkpoints or graph evidence to improve the product, will not qualify.
Track 1 — Build a Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience
Build a developer tool or workflow powered by context preserved in Entire Checkpoints. Git shows what changed; checkpoints should preserve why a change happened, what the agent attempted, which assumptions were made, what failed and what remains unresolved.
Review an implementation against its stated intent.
Identify unfinished requirements or unresolved risks.
Create a change-risk or release-readiness report.
Hand work to another developer or agent without losing the original reasoning.
Resume an agent-assisted workflow with confidence after a break.
Success looks like this: checkpoint context is an essential input, and a developer or agent completes a useful task more accurately or efficiently than they could from a Git diff alone.
Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence
Use the Entire Graph’s structural view of a codebase to support a useful decision or action. The graph can surface definitions, call relationships, types, routes and semantic changes. Your product must turn that evidence into a workflow that a developer or agent can inspect and verify.
Impact-aware code review or change-risk analysis.
Test selection based on affected relationships.
Migration planning or dependency-aware refactoring.
Codebase onboarding and guided exploration.
Combining Entire Graph findings with checkpoint intent.
Raw graph output is not enough. Your product should produce a useful decision, recommendation or workflow, show where the evidence came from, and let the user verify it against source code or tests.
Track 3 — Bring Entire to a New Agent or Workflow
Extend or create an Entire integration for a coding agent, editor, development environment, CI process or software-delivery workflow. The integration must capture meaningful development context and keep working in its intended operating mode.
Support for a new coding agent or editor workflow.
A CI or pull-request workflow that uses checkpoint context.
A multi-agent coordination workflow.
A protocol adapter between Entire and another developer tool.
External SDKs and fixtures are allowed, but the submitted implementation must live in the designated Entire fork. Calling an Entire command from another interface is not sufficient by itself.

Required Entire workflow
Complete these steps after the 9:00 AM kickoff. All implementation must happen in the clone created through the Entire mirror workflow.
1. Fork your selected repository
Fork the repository associated with your chosen track only after the Buildathon begins. Use existing issues for inspiration, or propose an original feature, integration or workflow.
2. Sign in and create the mirror
entire login
entire repo mirror create
entire repo clone /gh/YOUR-GITHUB-HANDLE/REPOSITORY
Select your fork and the India region when prompted. Clone through Entire, then work inside that clone.
3. Enable checkpoints
entire enable -y --agent YOUR-BUILD-AGENT
entire status
Commit meaningful milestones so code and context remain connected. Your checkpoint history must include at least:
Initial understanding and intended architecture.
The last stable state before the Noon Curveball.
Your response to the Noon Curveball.
Final implementation and verification.
Checkpoint quality matters more than quantity. Capture decisions, rejected options, failures, assumptions, open risks and the evidence that changed your approach.
4. Activate Entire Graph
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .
Start a fresh agent session after activation so the agent receives the graph instructions. During development, show at least:
A graph search or definition lookup.
A relationship or impact analysis before a high-risk change.
A final semantic diff analysis of the submitted implementation.
Graph results are evidence, not an oracle. Verify findings against source code, tests and runtime behavior. Never present incomplete or uncertain graph output as a fact.

The Noon Curveball
At exactly 12:00 noon, every team receives an additional track-specific constraint that becomes mandatory. The first version is the proof of what you built. The second version is the proof that your process can absorb change without losing intent.
11:45 AM — preserve the stable state
Stop adding optional features and get the product back to a runnable state.
Commit the last stable version.
Create the required pre-noon Entire Checkpoint.
Record the current intent, architecture, completed work, unresolved work and important technical risks.
12:00 PM — receive the constraint
Stop implementation and close the current coding-agent session.
Receive the official Curveball from the organising team. Do not exchange cards or use another track’s instruction.
Start a fresh agent session and use checkpoint context to reconstruct the project before editing.
Run Entire Graph impact analysis before changing the affected area.
Implement the smallest complete response, test it and record the result in a new checkpoint.
What judges will look for
A strong response preserves the product’s core idea, changes a real architectural or reliability decision, uses checkpoint context accurately, uses graph evidence where relevant, remains testable and explains why the revised behavior can be trusted.
The Curveball’s specific instructions are intentionally not published in advance. Mentors and organisers must not disclose them before noon.

Competing for Best Use of Databricks
Databricks is an additional award category within the same project.
Free Edition setup
Each teammate may explore in an individual Databricks Free Edition workspace.
Choose one final workspace for the shared dataset, deployed app or endpoint and final demonstration.
Keep notebooks, app code, configuration and documentation in the shared Git repository. Never commit access tokens or credentials.
Name one deployment owner and test that the owner can sign in and open every required resource before judging.
Good scope for a one-day build
An AI app or agent using Databricks Apps, hosted foundation models, model serving or AI Search where available.
An analytics experience using notebooks, SQL, dashboards or Genie to answer a concrete question.
A data pipeline that ingests, cleans and transforms representative data into a useful result.
A data-backed application using Lakehouse data and Databricks Apps for the user experience.
An ML experiment that uses a reproducible dataset, experiment tracking and an evaluation result.
Free Edition constraints to design around
Area
Planning constraint
Service model
No-cost, serverless, quota-limited environment for non-commercial learning and prototyping; no production SLA.
SQL and jobs
One serverless 2X-Small SQL warehouse; up to five concurrent job tasks per account.
Pipelines
One active pipeline per supported pipeline type.
Models and AI Search
Endpoint, throughput and model availability limits apply; no GPU or provisioned throughput; AI Search is limited.
Apps and database
Up to three Apps, with idle auto-stop behavior; one Lakebase project where available.
Workspace
One workspace and one metastore per account; several account-level and enterprise controls are unavailable.
Quota
When quota is exhausted, affected compute may be unavailable for the rest of the day or month. Build and test your narrow path early.


Work locally when practical, deploy one narrow slice early and preserve a screenshot or recording of any fragile live step. If live infrastructure fails during judging, explain the expected behavior, show the prepared evidence and continue with the product story.
Databricks Free Edition overview
Current Databricks Free Edition limitations
Responsible use of AI and data
Do not upload confidential company information, customer data, passwords, private keys or personal data that you do not have permission to use.
Do not put secrets in prompts, source repositories, screenshots, checkpoint context or BUILDATHON.md.
Verify generated code, SQL, citations and outputs. Test the cases that matter to your user and disclose what remains unverified.
Explain your data sources, permitted use, sampling or transformation, and important limitations.
Clearly label synthetic, cached, mocked or prototype data and responses.
You remain accountable for the implementation, even when a coding agent created it. Every teammate presenting should understand the relevant code and product decisions.

Final 20-minute checklist
The final commit is pushed and the SHA matches the submission.
The project launches from a clean checkout or the documented setup path.
Required checkpoints open and clearly explain the four milestones.
Entire Graph evidence and the final semantic-diff analysis are recorded.
BUILDATHON.md is complete, readable and free of secrets.
Tests covering the critical and Curveball behavior pass.
Databricks resource links and data notes are included if you opted in.
The demo owner can sign in, open every resource and run the critical path.
A fallback screenshot or recording is locally available.
The submission is sent before 3:00 PM IST.

Code of Conduct and safety
All participants must follow the Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct. Treat teammates, organisers, mentors, judges, venue staff and other participants with respect. Report harassment, unsafe behavior, accessibility barriers or urgent welfare issues to the event desk. For non-urgent questions, write to hello@bengalurutechweek.com.
Read the Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct



Submission package
Submit one project before 3:00 PM IST. Late or incomplete submissions may not reach judging. Open every link in a private or signed-out browser where appropriate, and make sure judges have the access they need without receiving a private credential.
Required submission fields
Selected Entire track.
GitHub fork URL and final commit SHA.
Entire mirror or project URL.
Links to the required Entire Checkpoints.
Clear setup, run and test instructions.
Working product demonstration or a reliable fallback recording.
A complete BUILDATHON.md file in the repository root.
If opting into Best Use of Databricks: the Databricks capabilities used, why they are essential, workspace/app/endpoint/demo URL, relevant repository paths, reproduction steps, data provenance and how the Curveball affected the Databricks workflow.

BULDATHON.md outline
# Project name
## One-sentence summary
## Problem, intended user and why it matters
## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
## Architecture and main workflow
## Entire Graph findings and verification
## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
## Setup, run and test instructions
## Databricks use, data sources and limitations (if applicable)
## Known limitations and next steps

Final demo readiness
State the user and problem in one sentence.
Show the working product and the critical path, rather than a slide-only walkthrough.
Explain why Entire is essential to the solution.
Show one useful checkpoint and one graph finding that changed or verified a decision.
Explain the Noon Curveball, the behavior that changed and the test that proves it.
If opting into Databricks, show the essential Databricks function and the evidence that it is working.
Close with known limitations and the next step toward production readiness.



How projects are judged
Entire main challenge — 100 points
Criterion
Points
What strong evidence shows
Problem and innovation
20
Clear user, specific problem, useful new capability and a real use of Entire.
Technical implementation
25
Working end-to-end workflow, sensible architecture, important behaviors tested and failures handled safely.
Response to the Curveball
15
Constraint addressed completely; assumptions revisited; response implemented, tested and explained.
Use of Entire Checkpoints
15
Checkpoints preserve useful intent and decision context; the fresh session can resume from them.
Use of Entire Graph
15
Graph evidence identifies relevant code or impact; findings are verified against source and tests.
Demonstration and future potential
10
Clear, reproducible demo; limits acknowledged; credible next step.


Best Use of Databricks — 100 points
Criterion
Points
What strong evidence shows
Meaningful use
30
Databricks is essential to a core workflow and materially improves what the product can do.
Working implementation and reliability
25
Judges can reproduce or inspect the path; failure handling and fallback evidence are credible.
User value and product decisions
20
Specific user need, focused scope and sensible trade-offs.
Data quality, provenance and responsible use
15
Permitted data, traceable transformations, disclosed limits and safe handling.
Curveball response
10
The Databricks-backed workflow adapts to the new constraint and the changed behavior is verified.

Enable Entire with session tracking for your AI agent workflows.

If Entire is not yet configured, this runs the full configuration flow.
If Entire is already configured but disabled, this re-enables it.

If the current directory is not a git repository, Entire can initialize one
for you and (optionally) create a matching GitHub repository via the gh CLI.

Usage:
  entire enable [flags]

Flags:
      --absolute-git-hook-path               Embed full binary path in git hooks (for GUI git clients that don't source shell profiles)
      --agent string                         Agent to set up hooks for (e.g., claude-code, codex, copilot-cli, cursor, factoryai-droid, gemini, opencode, pi; external agents on $PATH are also available). Enables non-interactive mode.
      --agent-help-skill entire agent-help   Install the stable Entire agent-help skill (points agents at entire agent-help) for selected agent(s)
      --checkpoint-backend string            Checkpoint storage backend: refs (default; one git ref per checkpoint) or branch (legacy shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)
      --checkpoint-remote string             Checkpoint remote in provider:owner/repo format (e.g., github:org/checkpoints-repo)
  -f, --force                                Force reinstall hooks (removes existing Entire hooks first)
  -h, --help                                 help for enable
      --import-history                       During first-time setup, import the selected agents' existing session history (last 30 days) without prompting
      --init-repo                            If not a git repo, initialize one non-interactively
      --initial-commit-message string        Commit message for the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --local                                Write settings to .entire/settings.local.json instead of .entire/settings.json
      --no-github                            Initialize local git repo only; skip creating a GitHub remote
      --no-init-repo                         If not a git repo, exit instead of prompting to initialize one
      --project                              Write settings to .entire/settings.json even if it already exists
      --push                                 When bootstrapping a new repo, push the initial commit to the created GitHub remote (implies creating the remote; without it the repo is created but not pushed)
      --repo-name string                     GitHub repository name for the new repo (used when bootstrapping)
      --repo-owner string                    GitHub user or organization login for the new repo
      --repo-visibility string               GitHub repository visibility: public, private, or internal
      --search-skill                         Install the optional Entire search skill for selected agent(s)
      --skip-initial-commit                  Don't create the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --skip-push-sessions                   Disable automatic pushing of session logs on git push
      --telemetry                            Enable anonymous usage analytics (default true)
  -y, --yes                                  Accept all defaults without prompting (in a non-repo directory: init git, create private GitHub repo, commit, and push; then enable all agents and accept telemetry). Does not import existing agent history — see --import-history

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

# Buildathon 2026 — Handoff (Entire Track 1: Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience)

## Context

Bengaluru Tech Week Buildathon, single-day event, solo entrant (Adit Potta / github.com/Aditaro). Must build on exactly one Entire track; committed to **Track 1: Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience** (registration constraint — only track available to commit to). Optional secondary "Best Use of Databricks" award is in scope (opted in).

This document is a **pre-event plan only**. Per the brief's pre-9AM rules, no implementation, scaffolding, or reusable code may exist before the Buildathon officially starts and the track repo is forked. Everything below is research, framing, and sequencing to execute quickly once the clock starts — not a head start.

Background that shaped this plan:
- GitHub history (`DB_LLM`: schema-aware NL→SQL assistant; `Sports ScoreHub`: SvelteKit+FastAPI+Groq/OpenRouter app; `AD-AutoGPT-Report`: agent experimentation) shows strong "NL interface over a structured/relational model" pattern and LLM-agent building experience — the design below reuses that pattern.
- Verified against real Entire docs (entire.io, github.com/entireio/cli) rather than trusting the brief's commands verbatim — see Setup section for corrections.
- User has ~$100 in Codex (OpenAI) credits to spend on this build — used both as a second coding agent and as the runtime LLM budget for the product itself.

## Product: "Handoff"

**One-liner:** Handoff mines Entire checkpoint history and generates a structured onboarding briefing so a fresh agent session — yours at the Noon Curveball, a teammate's, or an unrelated developer's — can reconstruct full project context in seconds instead of re-reading raw transcripts.

**Why this is differentiated, not a rehash:** the brief's own Curveball step says *"start a fresh agent session, reconstruct project understanding from checkpoint context before editing anything."* Most teams will treat that as a manual chore and build passive browsing/timeline tools. Handoff automates exactly that reconstruction step and is **self-demoing** — you run it on your own project at 12:00 to survive your own Curveball, live, on stage.

**Core mined signal — "landmines":** decisions that were reversed or thrashed on more than once across checkpoints. This is only extractable from checkpoint reasoning (prompts, rejected options, assumptions) — never from a plain git diff — so it's a genuinely checkpoint-native feature, not tracking-for-tracking's-sake.

## Architecture

**Pipeline:**
1. Pull checkpoint data: `entire checkpoint list --json`, then `entire checkpoint explain <id> --json` per checkpoint (transcripts, prompts, files touched, decisions/rejected-options text).
2. LLM synthesis pass (see Runtime LLM below) extracts structured JSON: `architecture_summary`, `current_state`, `unresolved_risks`, `landmines: [{file, symbol, description, times_reversed}]`.
3. Graph enrichment (mandatory deliverable, supporting evidence only): run the event's `entire graph` impact-analysis command against the most recently touched symbols/files, attach as a labeled evidence block. Design must degrade gracefully if the graph plugin isn't available/working — never assert graph output as fact per the brief's own warning.
4. Render `HANDOFF.md` at repo root (or `.entire-handoff/latest.md`) — the artifact a fresh session reads first.
5. Push the same structured JSON as one row into a Databricks Delta table for durable analytics (see Databricks below).

**Agent split (solo throughput, using both Claude Code and Codex):**
- **Claude Code** (Entire checkpoints enabled on it — `entire enable --agent claude-code`) drives the core Handoff CLI: checkpoint fetching, landmine-mining prompt logic, graph enrichment, `HANDOFF.md` rendering. This is the main workflow whose checkpoint history becomes your judged "Use of Entire Checkpoints" evidence, so it must stay the primary, git-integrated loop.
- **Codex** (funded by the $100 credit) drives the more self-contained Databricks workstream in parallel: the ingestion script and the SQL dashboard/notebook definition. Keep this loosely coupled (reads the same JSON schema Handoff produces) so it doesn't block or get blocked by the Claude Code loop.
- **Runtime LLM backend for the synthesis step itself:** use the OpenAI API (same $100 credit pool) as the primary model for step 2's extraction — a single well-tested prompt against a small/cheap model (e.g. a `gpt-4o-mini`-class model) is enough; keep a Groq or Claude fallback only if time allows, not required for MVP.

**Databricks piece (Best Use award):**
- Pre-event: create Databricks Free Edition account, verify sign-in (this is an allowed pre-9AM logistics task).
- On day: one 2X-Small serverless SQL warehouse (Free Edition quota: only one allowed). Create a Delta table, e.g. `handoff.briefings(session_id, branch, ts, architecture_summary, unresolved_risks, landmines, thrash_score, repo)`.
- Ingestion: a small Python script (Codex-built) using `databricks-sql-connector` to `INSERT` a row after each `handoff generate` run. Skip building a full Databricks App unless time is abundant — a script is enough to make the award's "meaningful use" bar and preserves quota.
- Dashboard: one Databricks SQL dashboard/notebook querying `handoff.briefings` — panels for landmine count over time, thrash hotspots by file, checkpoint cadence. This is the essential, durable analytics layer the CLI briefing alone can't provide (argument for "essential," not "used only for tracking").
- Never commit Databricks tokens/credentials to the repo — env vars only, verified before final submission.

## Noon Curveball fit

At 11:45 reach a stable state and commit the required pre-noon checkpoint (intent, architecture, completed/unresolved work, risks). At 12:00, close the session, receive the constraint, and — before touching code — **run Handoff on your own project** in the fresh session to reconstruct context. This is the live, meta demo: your own submission solving the exact problem the brief poses. Then run an Entire Graph impact analysis on the affected area before implementing the constraint, implement the smallest complete response, test it, and record the result in a new checkpoint.

## Entire setup (verified against real docs, corrections to the brief noted)

Pre-arrival (allowed now):
- Install: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash` (or `brew install --cask entire`)
- `entire login` (browser or `--device` flow) — authentication only, not tied to any repo, safe to do before kickoff

At/after kickoff (only after the fork exists):
- `entire repo mirror` / `entire repo clone` — follow the brief's literal `mirror create` / `clone /gh/<handle>/<repo>` steps; the public docs show slightly different subcommand names, so this may be event-customized — run `entire --help` or `entire doctor` if a subcommand doesn't match
- **`entire enable --agent claude-code`** (note: not `entire enable -y --agent ...` as the brief has it — `claude-code` is the correct, first-class supported agent value). This writes hooks into `.claude/settings.json` automatically.
- `entire status`, `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain <id>` — used both for compliance and as Handoff's own data source
- `entire plugin install graph`, then `entire graph version` to confirm — verified against `entireio/entire-graph` source. `entire graph init-agents --repo .` creates `.entire/graph-agent.md` and adds a managed block to `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. Start a **fresh** agent session after this — a session open during activation hasn't seen the new instructions.
  - Query commands (verified, not guessed): `entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<question>"` and `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol <Name>` — these are what Handoff's graph-enrichment step should shell out to.
- For the Codex agent workstream: `entire agent add codex` (or equivalent — verify with `entire agent --help`) if you want Codex's activity checkpointed too; otherwise Codex can work on the Databricks piece outside Entire's checkpoint scope since that piece isn't part of the judged checkpoint story.

## Testing / verification

No tests can be written before kickoff (would count as reusable implementation code). Plan for after 9:00:
- Unit-test the landmine miner's JSON extraction against checkpoints generated live during the build (not synthetic fixtures prepared in advance).
- End-to-end test: generate a `HANDOFF.md`, hand it to a genuinely fresh Claude Code session, confirm it can resume work without reading raw transcripts.
- At submission, capture the three required graph evidence artifacts (search/lookup, impact analysis before the Curveball change, final semantic diff) as part of `BUILDATHON.md`.

## Databricks account setup (do before arrival)

1. Sign up for Databricks Free Edition (search "Databricks Free Edition" from the official site if the exact signup link isn't already bookmarked — don't guess a deep link).
2. Verify workspace sign-in works and note the workspace URL.
3. Do not provision the SQL warehouse or table until the event's build window — quota is limited and burns from first use.

## Ponytail: AI Agent Coding Tool

Ponytail is an AI-agent ruleset and plugin system that pushes coding assistants toward simpler, smaller, and less over-engineered solutions, built around the idea that the best code is often the code that does not need to be written.

### Key Features

Agents tend to reach for a library or a custom component when a built in feature already does the job, and Ponytail checks the cheaper options first, in a fixed order, before it writes anything new. The tool delivers 80-94% less code, 47-77% less cost, and 3-6× faster results than a no-skill agent, on every model.

### Platform Support

The project supports several agent environments, including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and other instruction-based editors through copied rules files.

### Installation

For Copilot CLI, you can use the marketplace commands to add and install ponytail, which then injects the ruleset every turn at the active level and adds the /ponytail commands.

### Repository

The main project is located at **https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail** with the project having 68,000+ stars on GitHub.

content.text:
Quick answers on all four, since a couple of these carry real risk for a judged submission:

**Can opencode/Codex be Claude Code "subagents"?** No — Claude Code's Agent tool only spawns Claude-model agents (its built-in types or custom `.claude/agents/*.md` ones); it can't wrap a different CLI as a subagent type. What you *can* do — and what we already planned — is run opencode or Codex as separate, independent CLI processes on their own workstreams (that's exactly how Codex is slotted in for the Databricks piece). It's parallel orchestration, not literal subagenting.

**Graphify** — skip this one for the submission. I looked it up: it's literally a *competing* codebase-graph tool that shows up in Entire's own graph-plugin benchmark table as a rival to `entire graph`. Using it instead of (or alongside) Entire Graph risks reading as routing around the mandatory graph requirement — the guide explicitly disqualifies "adding Entire only for tracking... without using its graph evidence." Not worth the risk today.

**OmniRoute** — skip it too, but for a practical reason: it's a self-hosted multi-provider LLM gateway/proxy. You'd be adding an extra service, extra API-key juggling across 300+ providers, on a one-day build where you already have Claude + $100 in OpenAI/Codex credits covering everything you need. It solves a quota-diversity problem you don't have yet.

**Ponytail** — this one's worth taking. It's a lightweight ruleset/skill (not infra) that pushes coding agents toward less code, no unnecessary dependencies, checking built-ins before writing new things — directly reinforces the "narrow slice, YAGNI" discipline the plan already calls for. Low risk, quick install, works across Claude Code/Codex/opencode.

Want me to go ahead and set up Ponytail for the agents now (safe, no repo needed yet), and do you want opencode running as a genuine third parallel workstream, or keep it in reserve for now given it's just you managing all three?

# Ponytail Installation: Claude Code & OpenCode

## Claude Code

**Setup commands:**
```
/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
/plugin install ponytail@ponytail
```

Note: "You have to send two separate prompts for the install to work"

**Verification:** The plugin activates automatically. Use `/ponytail` to check the current mode level (defaults to `full`).

**Files created/modified:**
- `~/.config/ponytail/config.json` (optional, for setting `defaultMode`)
- `~/.claude/settings.json` (adds a `statusLine` entry if you accept the setup nudge)

---

## OpenCode

**Setup:** Add to your project's `opencode.json`:
```json
{ "plugin": ["@dietrichgebert/ponytail"] }
```

**Verification:** The ruleset injects automatically on every turn. Type `/ponytail` commands (lite/full/ultra/off) into chat to confirm activation and mode switching.

**Files created/modified:**
- Your project's `opencode.json` (adds the plugin reference)
- The plugin registers `/ponytail` commands and loads the `AGENTS.md` ruleset automatically

**Alternative (local checkout):**
```json
{ "plugin": ["./.opencode/plugins/ponytail.mjs"] }
```
This reuses the repo's `hooks/` and `skills/` directories.

# OpenAI Provider Configuration in OpenCode

## Setup Steps

1. **Authenticate via `/connect`:**
   ```
   /connect
   ```
   Select OpenAI, then choose either "ChatGPT Plus/Pro" (browser OAuth) or "Manually enter API Key"

2. **API Key Method:**
   If using manual entry, paste your OpenAI API key when prompted.

## Configuration File

Add to `opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "gpt-5",
  "provider": {
    "openai": {
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://api.openai.com/v1"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Key Details

- **Config location:** Project directory as `opencode.json`
- **Base URL:** The documentation states: `"baseURL": "https://api.openai.com/v1"` can customize the endpoint
- **Model selection:** Use `/models` command to view available options; set preferred model via `"model"` field in config
- **No environment variables required** for OpenAI when using `/connect` (credentials stored automatically)

## Model Selection

Available top-tier models appear in the `/models` picker. Set your default by specifying the model ID in your configuration file's root `"model"` property.

content.content:
# Graphify OpenCode Setup

## OpenCode Support

Yes, Graphify explicitly supports OpenCode. According to the documentation, OpenCode is listed among 20+ supported platforms.

## Installation Steps

**Step 1 — Install the package:**

```bash
uv tool install graphifyy
# OR
pipx install graphifyy
```

**Step 2 — Register with OpenCode:**

```bash
graphify install --platform opencode
```

## What Gets Modified

The installation writes an `AGENTS.md` file to your project and a `tool.execute.before` plugin configuration. The documentation states: "OpenCode uses sequential extraction (parallel agent support is still early on those platforms)."

## Verification

After installation, you can verify it's working by:

1. Running `/graphify .` in your OpenCode assistant
2. Checking that three output files appear in `graphify-out/`:
   - `graph.html` (interactive visualization)
   - `GRAPH_REPORT.md` (highlights and analysis)
   - `graph.json` (queryable knowledge graph)

## How It Works

Unlike some platforms, OpenCode uses an instruction-file approach rather than hooks. The generated `AGENTS.md` provides persistent guidance to query the graph for codebase questions, preferring scoped queries like `graphify query "<question>"` over raw file grepping.

# OmniRoute + OpenCode Setup Instructions

## Installation

Install OmniRoute globally via npm:

```bash
npm install -g omniroute
```

The gateway automatically starts on `localhost:20128/v1` after installation with zero configuration required.

## Pointing OpenCode at OmniRoute

OpenCode is configured to use OmniRoute as its backend by setting the API endpoint. Use this base URL:

```
http://localhost:20128/v1
```

For the OpenCode integration specifically, OmniRoute provides a native plugin. Install it with:

```bash
npm install @omniroute/opencode-provider
```

Then configure OpenCode to use the OmniRoute provider through the plugin system.

## Verification

Test the connection with a simple curl request:

```bash
curl http://localhost:20128/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"auto","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}]}'
```

The gateway responds immediately using the `auto` model (which routes to available free providers like OpenCode Zen) without requiring any API keys or additional setup.

For full CLI integration details and per-tool configuration, see the [CLI Integrations documentation](https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/release/v3.8.51/docs/guides/CLI-INTEGRATIONS.md) in the project repository.

---
title: "OpenCode Integration"
version: 3.8.40
lastUpdated: 2027-07-27
---

# OpenCode Integration

> **Status:** Generally available.
> **Audience:** Operators wiring OpenCode to an OmniRoute deployment.
> **Source of truth (config schema):** `src/shared/services/opencodeConfig.ts`
> **Source of truth (npm package):** `@omniroute/opencode-provider/` (publishable workspace)

[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) is an agentic CLI/desktop AI client. It reads its provider catalog from `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (or `opencode.jsonc`) and follows the schema at `https://opencode.ai/config.json`. OmniRoute exposes itself to OpenCode as one of those providers — every request flows through OmniRoute's standard OpenAI-compatible `/v1` surface, so OpenCode automatically benefits from Auto-Combo routing, circuit breakers, key policies, observability, etc.

There are **two supported integration paths**. Pick one — they generate the same config.

---

## Path 1 — CLI generator (no npm install)

Recommended for end users. Ships with OmniRoute. Writes `opencode.json` in place.

```bash
# After installing OmniRoute (npm i -g @omniroute/cli or local clone)
omniroute config opencode \
  --base-url http://localhost:20128 \
  --api-key "$OMNIROUTE_API_KEY"
```

Behind the scenes the CLI calls `mergeOpenCodeConfigText()` (`src/shared/services/opencodeConfig.ts:104`), so an existing `opencode.json` keeps its other providers and comments. The OmniRoute entry is added/replaced atomically.

Resulting file (default model catalog):

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "omniroute": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "OmniRoute",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://localhost:20128/v1",
        "apiKey": "<your-key>",
      },
      "models": {
        "claude-opus-4-5-thinking": { "name": "claude-opus-4-5-thinking" },
        "claude-sonnet-4-5-thinking": { "name": "claude-sonnet-4-5-thinking" },
        "gemini-3.1-pro-high": { "name": "gemini-3.1-pro-high" },
        "gemini-3-flash": { "name": "gemini-3-flash" },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

---

## Path 2 — npm package `@omniroute/opencode-provider`

Recommended when you're scripting the config from Node/TS (CI pipelines, monorepos, custom installer flows).

```bash
npm install --save-dev @omniroute/opencode-provider
```

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { buildOmniRouteOpenCodeConfig } from "@omniroute/opencode-provider";

const config = buildOmniRouteOpenCodeConfig({
  baseURL: "http://localhost:20128",
  apiKey: process.env.OMNIROUTE_API_KEY ?? "sk_omniroute",
  // Optional: override the model catalog exposed to OpenCode
  models: ["auto", "claude-opus-4-7", "gpt-5.5"],
  modelLabels: { auto: "Auto-Combo" },
});

writeFileSync("opencode.json", JSON.stringify(config, null, 2));
```

For a non-destructive merge against an existing file, replicate `mergeOpenCodeConfigText()` from `opencodeConfig.ts` or call the CLI generator.

See the [package README](../../@omniroute/opencode-provider/README.md) for the full API.

---

## What the runtime actually does

Both paths produce the same `provider.omniroute.npm: "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible"`. At runtime, OpenCode loads `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` (already a transitive dependency of OpenCode) and configures it with `baseURL` + `apiKey`. From there:

```
OpenCode UI/agent
   → @ai-sdk/openai-compatible
      → HTTP POST {baseURL}/chat/completions          (OmniRoute OpenAI surface)
         → OmniRoute /v1/chat/completions handler     (open-sse/handlers/chatCore.ts)
            → combo routing / Auto-Combo / executor
               → upstream provider
```

# Handoff

## One-sentence summary
Handoff mines Entire checkpoint history into a structured onboarding briefing so a fresh agent session can reconstruct full project context in seconds instead of re-reading raw transcripts.

## Problem, intended user and why it matters
Every agent-assisted workflow eventually forces a handoff: a session ends, a teammate picks up the work, or (as this Buildathon's own Noon Curveball requires) you deliberately start fresh and have to reconstruct intent before touching code. Git shows *what* changed; it doesn't show *why*, what was tried and rejected, or what's still unresolved. Developers and agents currently do this reconstruction by hand, re-reading raw transcripts or guessing from diffs. Handoff's user is any developer or agent that needs to resume someone else's (or their own past) work with confidence.

## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
**Track 1 — Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience.** Entire Checkpoints are not a logging side-effect here; they are Handoff's only source material. The "landmines" feature — decisions that were reversed or thrashed on more than once — is only extractable from checkpoint reasoning (prompts, rejected options, assumptions), never from a plain git diff. Without Entire, there is no product.

## Architecture and main workflow
1. Pull checkpoint data: `entire checkpoint list` / `entire checkpoint explain <id>`.
2. Synthesize structured JSON (architecture summary, current state, unresolved risks, landmines) via an LLM pass.
3. Enrich with Entire Graph evidence (`entire graph search`, `entire graph impact`) on recently touched symbols — shown as evidence, not asserted as fact.
4. Render `HANDOFF.md` for the next agent session to read first.
5. (Databricks) push the same structured record into a Delta table for durable, queryable decision-health analytics.

Build split: Claude Code drives the core, checkpointed workflow; opencode/Codex execute independent workstreams (Databricks ingestion + dashboard) under Claude Code's direction, coordinated via `TASKS.md` — itself a live demonstration of Track 1's "hand work to another agent without losing the original reasoning."

## Entire Graph findings and verification
_(to fill in during the build — will include one search/lookup, one pre-Curveball impact analysis, and the final semantic diff)_

## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
_(to fill in at/after 12:00)_

## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
_(to fill in — must cover: initial understanding/architecture, last stable pre-Curveball state, Curveball response, final implementation/verification)_

## Setup, run and test instructions
_(to fill in once Handoff's CLI exists)_

## Databricks use, data sources and limitations
_(to fill in if/as built — Free Edition, one Delta table `handoff.briefings`, one SQL dashboard)_

## Known limitations and next steps
_(to fill in before submission)_

content.text:
Fair question to stop and ask. Let me walk through it plainly.

**What Handoff actually does, concretely:** Say you've been coding for two hours with Claude Code enabled via Entire — 15 checkpoints accumulated. Someone (or a fresh agent, or you at the Curveball) needs to pick up the work with zero prior context. Today, that means reading raw transcripts or guessing from a git diff, which shows *what* changed but never *why*. You run `handoff generate`. It pulls every checkpoint (`entire checkpoint list` / `explain`), feeds the transcripts to an LLM, and produces one document: architecture summary, current state, unresolved risks, and "landmines" — things that were tried, reverted, and tried again, which is a signal that only exists in checkpoint reasoning, never in a diff. Optionally it appends a graph impact-analysis snippet on whatever was touched most recently. That's it. One command, one artifact, one real use of checkpoints that a diff can't replace.

**Does it win, by the actual rubric?**

| Criterion | Pts | Handoff's position |
|---|---|---|
| Problem & innovation | 20 | Strong — it's almost a direct restatement of Track 1's own named use cases ("hand work to another agent without losing reasoning," "resume with confidence after a break"). Not flashy, but unambiguously real. |
| Technical implementation | 25 | Unknown yet — depends entirely on whether we ship a working end-to-end slice. This is the biggest swing factor. |
| Curveball response | 15 | Naturally strong — Handoff is literally the tool for the exact moment the Curveball forces ("fresh session, reconstruct from checkpoints"). We can run it on ourselves, live. |
| Checkpoints | 15 | Strong by construction — checkpoints are Handoff's only input, not a bolt-on. |
| Graph | 15 | Solid if the enrichment step works — supporting evidence, not the core mechanic, which is honest given Track 1. |
| Demo & potential | 10 | Strong — self-referential live demo ("watch it reconstruct our own session, on stage") is genuinely rare. |

Add it up: **70 of 100 points are about execution and correct use of Entire, not idea novelty.** Problem/innovation is only 20. That's the honest answer to "is this what it takes to win" — at this point in the day, a solid-but-not-flashy idea that actually *works end-to-end and is well-checkpointed* will beat a more exciting idea that's half-built, because three-quarters of the score is graded on execution.

The uncomfortable part I should say directly: the real risk to winning right now isn't Handoff's idea quality — it's that we've spent ~1.5 hours on tooling (opencode, ponytail, omniroute, graphify, Entire setup) and haven't written a line of Handoff's actual code yet, with the pre-noon freeze at 11:45. That's the thing most likely to cost us points, not the choice of idea.

My honest read: Handoff clears the bar. Want me to lock it in and start building the narrowest working slice right now (checkpoint pull → LLM synthesis → `HANDOFF.md`), or is there a specific part of the idea itself that's still bugging you?

List checkpoints on the current branch.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for the resume view instead: live checkpoints on
the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed), plus logs-only resume points
recovered from commits whose logs are already condensed.

Output modes:
  --json             Machine-readable JSON instead of the human view.
  --pending          Select the pending dataset: live shadow-branch
                     checkpoints plus logs-only resume points.
  --pending --json   Pending checkpoints as JSON (replaces the deprecated rewind --list).

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending).

Usage:
  entire checkpoint list [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for list
      --json             Output as JSON instead of the human view
      --no-pager         Disable pager output
      --pending          List pending checkpoints — live shadow-branch state plus logs-only resume points
      --session string   Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Global Flags:

=== explain ===
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

Usage:
  entire checkpoint explain [checkpoint-id | commit-sha] [flags]

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint

      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (owner/name or gh/owner/name), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout

content.text:
Good problem to interrogate, even hypothetically. Here's the honest breakdown, same rubric-mapped approach as before:

**Is it a real problem worth solving?** Yes, genuinely. Database migrations breaking production is a well-known, high-stakes pain point, and "self-healing" (detect failure, auto-recover, explain why) is a real ambition companies pay for (see Bytebase, PlanetScale's whole business). Not a manufactured problem.

**How it'd score, if built well:**

| Criterion | Pts | vs. Handoff |
|---|---|---|
| Problem & innovation | 20 | **Higher ceiling.** "Self-healing migrations" is a more viscerally impressive pitch than "reads your checkpoints." |
| Technical implementation | 25 | **Much higher risk.** You'd need real failure-detection, real rollback logic, real Databricks Delta time-travel integration, all working — not mocked. This is a bigger engineering surface than Handoff by a wide margin. |
| Curveball response | 15 | Potentially strong — a curveball that changes a migration mid-day and watching the system catch it live is a compelling story, if it's real. |
| Checkpoints | 15 | **This is the trap.** If checkpoints just *log* the migration attempt while Databricks time-travel does 100% of the actual healing, that's decorative use of Entire — exactly what the guide's disqualification language targets ("adding Entire only for tracking... will not qualify"). To score well here, checkpoint context has to actually *decide* the healing action (e.g., "what was originally intended, per the checkpoint, before this migration went wrong"), which is the harder half of the build. |
| Graph | 15 | **Actually a cleaner fit than Handoff's.** "What depends on this schema before I change it" is closer to the graph's textbook use case than Handoff's supporting-evidence framing. |
| Demo & potential | 10 | **Higher ceiling.** "Watch it break on purpose and heal itself" beats a markdown document as theater. |

**Net verdict:** it has a higher ceiling on Problem/Innovation + Demo (30 pts combined) and arguably a cleaner Graph story, but it carries much higher execution risk on the single biggest bucket (Technical Implementation, 25 pts) and a real chance of landing in "Entire as decoration" territory on Checkpoints (15 pts) unless the self-healing decision logic is genuinely checkpoint-driven, not just checkpoint-logged — that's the part that separates "impressive demo" from "actually needed Entire." That last distinction is the hard engineering problem, not the migration mechanics themselves.

If you build it later without a clock: that's the thing to architect first — make the checkpoint the thing that decides the fix, not just the thing that records the attempt. That's already captured in the memory note I saved.

# Warden

## One-sentence summary
Warden is a self-healing database migration guard: it checkpoints a migration's intent before running it, and if the migration fails validation, it auto-rolls-back via Databricks Delta time-travel while explaining the failure using the original intent recorded in the checkpoint — not just "reverted."

## Problem, intended user and why it matters
Database migrations fail in production regularly, and when they do, the standard response is a blind revert with no memory of what the migration was actually trying to achieve. The developer picking up the failure has to reconstruct intent from scratch. Warden's user is any developer or team running schema/data migrations who wants automatic recovery that explains itself, not just a rollback.

## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
**Track 1 — Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience.** The healing decision is checkpoint-driven, not just checkpoint-logged: when a migration fails, Warden doesn't merely time-travel the Delta table back — it reads the pre-migration checkpoint's recorded intent to explain *why* the migration was attempted and what should have happened, then surfaces that alongside the rollback. Without the checkpoint, there is a revert with no explanation; with it, there is a recovery with reasoning. Entire Graph runs an impact analysis before the migration lands, so the blast radius is known before the risk is taken, not just after.

## Architecture and main workflow
1. `warden migrate <migration.sql>`:
   a. Write a pre-migration Entire checkpoint: intent (what's changing, why), files/schema touched.
   b. Run `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol <affected>` for a relationship/impact check before the change lands.
   c. Apply the migration to a Databricks Delta table.
   d. Run a validation check (schema/data-quality assertion).
   e. On failure: `RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF <n>` (Delta time-travel) to roll back, then read the pre-migration checkpoint's intent to generate a human-readable explanation of what was attempted and why it failed.
   f. Record the full attempt → failure → heal trail as a new Entire checkpoint.
2. Databricks is the substrate the whole mechanic depends on: Delta Lake's native versioning is the rollback primitive, and a SQL dashboard visualizes migration attempts/heals over time.

Build split: Claude Code drives the core Warden CLI and checkpoint logic; opencode/Codex build the Databricks Delta table setup, synthetic seed data, and dashboard in parallel, coordinated via `TASKS.md`.

## Entire Graph findings and verification
_(to fill in during the build — impact analysis before the demo migration, plus the final semantic diff)_

## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
_(to fill in at/after 12:00)_

## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
_(to fill in — includes the pivot checkpoint recording the move from the original "Handoff" concept to Warden, and why)_

## Setup, run and test instructions
_(to fill in once Warden's CLI exists)_

## Databricks use, data sources and limitations
Free Edition, one 2X-Small SQL warehouse, one Delta table for the demo migration target, synthetic/clearly-labeled seed data only. Delta time-travel is the rollback mechanism — this is why Databricks is essential, not incidental.

## Known limitations and next steps
_(to fill in before submission)_

Good question — not fully redundant, they serve different layers:

- **Entire checkpoints** = long-term memory. Rich, historical, tied to commits — great for "what happened and why," but you have to run a CLI command and parse output to get it. Retrospective by nature.
- **TASKS.md** = working memory. A live, instantly-readable snapshot of "what's happening right now across the three of us" — no CLI query needed, just open the file. Checkpoints don't give you that at-a-glance current-state view.

And practically they're not competing — TASKS.md is git-tracked, so every edit to it also becomes part of the checkpoint history automatically. It's not a parallel system, it's the fast front-door on top of the slower archival one. I'll keep using it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Warden: self-healing database migration guard for Databricks Delta tables.

Core loop: read the migration's intent from the most recent Entire checkpoint,
run an Entire Graph impact check, apply the migration, validate it, and on
failure roll back via Delta time-travel while explaining the failure using the
checkpoint's recorded intent -- not just a blind revert.

Synthetic/demo data only. Requires env vars:
  DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME, DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH, DATABRICKS_TOKEN
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys


def run_entire(args, timeout=30):
    """Run an `entire` subcommand, returning stdout. Never raises -- degrades
    gracefully with a note, per the Buildathon guide's own warning that graph
    (and checkpoint) output is evidence, not fact, and must not be presented
    as certain when it can't be obtained."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["entire"] + args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout
        )
        if result.returncode != 0:
            return None, result.stderr.strip()
        return result.stdout, None
    except Exception as e:
        return None, str(e)


def get_latest_checkpoint():
    """Returns (checkpoint_id, intent_text) for the most recent checkpoint on
    this branch, or (None, None) if unavailable."""
    out, err = run_entire(["checkpoint", "list", "--json"])
    if out is None:
        print(f"[warden] WARNING: could not list checkpoints ({err}); proceeding without recorded intent")
        return None, None
    try:
        checkpoints = json.loads(out)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print("[warden] WARNING: checkpoint list did not parse as JSON; proceeding without recorded intent")
        return None, None
    if not checkpoints:
        return None, None
    cp_id = checkpoints[0]["checkpoint_id"]
    explain, err = run_entire(["checkpoint", "explain", cp_id, "--short", "--no-pager"])
    if explain is None:
        print(f"[warden] WARNING: could not explain checkpoint {cp_id} ({err})")
        return cp_id, None
    return cp_id, explain.strip()


def graph_impact(symbol):
    """Best-effort Entire Graph impact analysis. Evidence, not fact -- shown
    to the operator, never asserted as ground truth."""
    out, err = run_entire(["graph", "impact", "--repo", ".", "--symbol", symbol], timeout=30)
    if out is None:
        return f"(graph impact unavailable: {err})"
    return out.strip()


def connect():
    from databricks import sql
    missing = [v for v in ("DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME", "DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH", "DATABRICKS_TOKEN") if v not in os.environ]
    if missing:
        print(f"[warden] ERROR: missing required env vars: {', '.join(missing)}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    return sql.connect(
        server_hostname=os.environ["DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME"],
        http_path=os.environ["DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH"],
        access_token=os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"],
    )


def current_delta_version(cur, table):
    cur.execute(f"DESCRIBE HISTORY {table} LIMIT 1")
    row = cur.fetchone()
    return row[0]


def ensure_log_table(cur):
    cur.execute(
        """
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warden.migration_log (
            id STRING,
            migration_name STRING,
            status STRING,
            checkpoint_id STRING,
            note STRING,
            ts TIMESTAMP
        ) USING DELTA
        """
    )


def log_attempt(cur, migration_name, status, checkpoint_id, note):
    ensure_log_table(cur)
    cur.execute(
        """
        INSERT INTO warden.migration_log (id, migration_name, status, checkpoint_id, note, ts)
        VALUES (uuid(), ?, ?, ?, ?, current_timestamp())
        """,
        (migration_name, status, checkpoint_id or "", (note or "")[:4000]),
    )


def apply_migration(migration_path, table, validate_sql_path):
    with open(migration_path) as f:
        migration_sql = f.read()

    validate_sql = None
    if validate_sql_path:
        with open(validate_sql_path) as f:
            validate_sql = f.read().strip()

    cp_id, intent = get_latest_checkpoint()
    print(f"[warden] intent from checkpoint {cp_id or '(none)'}:\n{intent or '(unavailable)'}\n")

    symbol = table.split(".")[-1]
    impact = graph_impact(symbol)
    print(f"[warden] Entire Graph impact on '{symbol}' (evidence, not fact -- verify before trusting):\n{impact}\n")

    conn = connect()
    cur = conn.cursor()
    try:
        pre_version = current_delta_version(cur, table)
        print(f"[warden] '{table}' currently at Delta version {pre_version}")

        for stmt in migration_sql.split(";"):
            stmt = stmt.strip()
            if stmt:
                cur.execute(stmt)
        print(f"[warden] migration '{migration_path}' applied.")

        offending_rows = 0
        if validate_sql:
            cur.execute(validate_sql)
            offending_rows = len(cur.fetchall())
            print(f"[warden] validation {'passed' if offending_rows == 0 else 'FAILED'} ({offending_rows} offending row(s))")

        if offending_rows == 0:
            log_attempt(cur, migration_path, "success", cp_id, "applied cleanly, validation passed")
            print("[warden] SUCCESS.")
            return 0

        raise RuntimeError(f"validation failed: {offending_rows} row(s) violated the check in {validate_sql_path}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[warden] FAILURE: {e}")
        print(f"[warden] healing: restoring '{table}' to Delta version {pre_version} via time-travel...")
        cur.execute(f"RESTORE TABLE {table} TO VERSION AS OF {pre_version}")
        explanation = (
            f"Migration '{migration_path}' failed: {e}\n\n"
            f"Recorded intent (checkpoint {cp_id or 'unavailable'}):\n{intent or '(no intent recorded)'}\n\n"
            f"Action taken: rolled back {table} to Delta version {pre_version}. "
            f"The intent above is what this migration was trying to achieve -- "
            f"use it to write a corrected migration rather than re-attempting blindly."
        )
        print(f"\n[warden] {explanation}")
        log_attempt(cur, migration_path, "healed", cp_id, explanation)
        return 1
    finally:
        cur.close()
        conn.close()


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Warden: self-healing DB migration guard")
    parser.add_argument("migration", help="path to the migration .sql file")
    parser.add_argument("--table", default="warden.demo_users", help="target Delta table")
    parser.add_argument("--validate-sql", help="path to a SQL file returning offending rows (0 rows = pass)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    sys.exit(apply_migration(args.migration, args.table, args.validate_sql))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Warden: self-healing database migration guard for Databricks Delta tables.

Core loop: read the migration's intent from the most recent Entire checkpoint,
run an Entire Graph impact check, apply the migration, validate it, and on
failure roll back via Delta time-travel while explaining the failure using the
checkpoint's recorded intent -- not just a blind revert.

Synthetic/demo data only. Requires env vars:
  DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME, DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH, DATABRICKS_TOKEN
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys


def run_entire(args, timeout=30):
    """Run an `entire` subcommand, returning stdout. Never raises -- degrades
    gracefully with a note, per the Buildathon guide's own warning that graph
    (and checkpoint) output is evidence, not fact, and must not be presented
    as certain when it can't be obtained."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["entire"] + args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout
        )
        if result.returncode != 0:
            return None, result.stderr.strip()
        return result.stdout, None
    except Exception as e:
        return None, str(e)


def get_latest_checkpoint():
    """Returns (checkpoint_id, intent_text) for the most recent checkpoint on
    this branch, or (None, None) if unavailable."""
    out, err = run_entire(["checkpoint", "list", "--json"])
    if out is None:
        print(f"[warden] WARNING: could not list checkpoints ({err}); proceeding without recorded intent")
        return None, None
    try:
        checkpoints = json.loads(out)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print("[warden] WARNING: checkpoint list did not parse as JSON; proceeding without recorded intent")
        return None, None
    if not checkpoints:
        return None, None
    cp_id = checkpoints[0]["checkpoint_id"]
    explain, err = run_entire(["checkpoint", "explain", cp_id, "--short", "--no-pager"])
    if explain is None:
        print(f"[warden] WARNING: could not explain checkpoint {cp_id} ({err})")
        return cp_id, None
    return cp_id, explain.strip()


def graph_impact(symbol):
    """Best-effort Entire Graph impact analysis. Evidence, not fact -- shown
    to the operator, never asserted as ground truth."""
    out, err = run_entire(["graph", "impact", "--repo", ".", "--symbol", symbol], timeout=30)
    if out is None:
        return f"(graph impact unavailable: {err})"
    return out.strip()


def connect():
    from databricks import sql
    missing = [v for v in ("DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME", "DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH", "DATABRICKS_TOKEN") if v not in os.environ]
    if missing:
        print(f"[warden] ERROR: missing required env vars: {', '.join(missing)}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    return sql.connect(
        server_hostname=os.environ["DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME"],
        http_path=os.environ["DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH"],
        access_token=os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"],
    )


def current_delta_version(cur, table):
    cur.execute(f"DESCRIBE HISTORY {table} LIMIT 1")
    row = cur.fetchone()
    return row[0]


def ensure_log_table(cur):
    cur.execute(
        """
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warden.migration_log (
            id STRING,
            migration_name STRING,
            status STRING,
            checkpoint_id STRING,
            note STRING,
            ts TIMESTAMP
        ) USING DELTA
        """
    )


def log_attempt(cur, migration_name, status, checkpoint_id, note):
    ensure_log_table(cur)
    cur.execute(
        """
        INSERT INTO warden.migration_log (id, migration_name, status, checkpoint_id, note, ts)
        VALUES (uuid(), ?, ?, ?, ?, current_timestamp())
        """,
        (migration_name, status, checkpoint_id or "", (note or "")[:4000]),
    )


def apply_migration(migration_path, table, validate_sql_path):
    with open(migration_path) as f:
        migration_sql = f.read()

    validate_sql = None
    if validate_sql_path:
        with open(validate_sql_path) as f:
            validate_sql = f.read().strip()

    cp_id, intent = get_latest_checkpoint()
    print(f"[warden] intent from checkpoint {cp_id or '(none)'}:\n{intent or '(unavailable)'}\n")

    symbol = table.split(".")[-1]
    impact = graph_impact(symbol)
    print(f"[warden] Entire Graph impact on '{symbol}' (evidence, not fact -- verify before trusting):\n{impact}\n")

    conn = connect()
    cur = conn.cursor()
    try:
        pre_version = current_delta_version(cur, table)
        print(f"[warden] '{table}' currently at Delta version {pre_version}")

        for stmt in migration_sql.split(";"):
            stmt = stmt.strip()
            if stmt:
                cur.execute(stmt)
        print(f"[warden] migration '{migration_path}' applied.")

        offending_rows = 0
        if validate_sql:
            cur.execute(validate_sql)
            offending_rows = len(cur.fetchall())
            print(f"[warden] validation {'passed' if offending_rows == 0 else 'FAILED'} ({offending_rows} offending row(s))")

        if offending_rows == 0:
            log_attempt(cur, migration_path, "success", cp_id, "applied cleanly, validation passed")
            print("[warden] SUCCESS.")
            return 0

        raise RuntimeError(f"validation failed: {offending_rows} row(s) violated the check in {validate_sql_path}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[warden] FAILURE: {e}")
        print(f"[warden] healing: restoring '{table}' to Delta version {pre_version} via time-travel...")
        cur.execute(f"RESTORE TABLE {table} TO VERSION AS OF {pre_version}")
        explanation = (
            f"Migration '{migration_path}' failed: {e}\n\n"
            f"Recorded intent (checkpoint {cp_id or 'unavailable'}):\n{intent or '(no intent recorded)'}\n\n"
            f"Action taken: rolled back {table} to Delta version {pre_version}. "
            f"The intent above is what this migration was trying to achieve -- "
            f"use it to write a corrected migration rather than re-attempting blindly."
        )
        print(f"\n[warden] {explanation}")
        log_attempt(cur, migration_path, "healed", cp_id, explanation)
        return 1
    finally:
        cur.close()
        conn.close()


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Warden: self-healing DB migration guard")
    parser.add_argument("migration", help="path to the migration .sql file")
    parser.add_argument("--table", default="warden.demo_users", help="target Delta table")
    parser.add_argument("--validate-sql", help="path to a SQL file returning offending rows (0 rows = pass)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    sys.exit(apply_migration(args.migration, args.table, args.validate_sql))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.content:
One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol

Usage:
  entire graph impact --symbol NAME|<file>:<line> --repo . [--depth 1|2] [--limit 15] [--format text|json]

Everything the graph knows about changing one symbol in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth <=2), callees, type consumers (USES_TYPE/PARAM_TYPE/RETURNS_TYPE), data flows, files that historically co-change with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Run this before changing a function/type's behavior.

Ambiguous names return the definition list; rerun with --file/--line/--kind (or --symbol <file>:<line>) to pick one.

Flags:
  --symbol NAME|<file>:<line>
                            Symbol to analyze (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository (default: current repo)
  --file <path>             Disambiguate an ambiguous name by file
  --line <n>                Disambiguate by line
  --kind <kind>             Disambiguate by symbol kind
  --depth 1|2               Caller-traversal depth (default: 2)
  --limit <n>               Max entries per section (default: 15)
  --format text|json        Output format
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Total text budget (default: 4096)
  --exclude-tests           Drop test-only entries
  --head                    Query the committed tree (cached)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth (default: full)

Examples:
  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol WriteText
=== search help ===
entire graph adds a deterministic, no-egress code graph to Entire checkpoints.

Usage:
  entire graph <command> [flags]

Set up your agent:
  init-agents      Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
  agent-guide      Print the coding-agent operating guide
  index            Build/warm a committed-tree cache variant for matching queries
  capabilities     List parsed languages, relation types, and features

Inspect the graph:
  search           Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)
  neighbors        Who calls this / what does it call (targeted relations)
  impact           One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol
  def              What a name IS: declaration, fields, and method surface
  explain          Resolve symbols named by a failing build or test
  symbols          Stream every symbol definition (bulk NDJSON)
  edges            Stream every relation (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot         Stream the whole graph: files, symbols, and relations (bulk NDJSON)
  snapshot-query   Query a compact snapshot without rebuilding the graph

Analyze changes & more:
  commit           Entity-level change list for a commit vs its first parent
  diff             Entity-level change list between two refs
  checkpoint       Analyze the commit behind an Entire-Checkpoint trailer
  verify           Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output
  stats            Human report: graph usage vs grep/read, and estimated token savings

Help & diagnostics:
  help             Show this command listing
  doctor           Diagnose the environment and confirm no-egress
  version          Print the plugin version (and provider name with --json)

Use "entire graph <command> --help" for details on a command.
For coding agents: run "entire graph agent-guide" or "entire graph init-agents".

"""Unit tests for Warden's checkpoint/graph logic (no live Databricks needed).

Run: python3 -m pytest warden/test_migrate.py -v
"""
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))
from migrate import get_latest_checkpoint, graph_impact, run_entire  # noqa: E402


def _fake_run(returncode=0, stdout="", stderr=""):
    return subprocess.CompletedProcess(args=[], returncode=returncode, stdout=stdout, stderr=stderr)


def test_get_latest_checkpoint_skips_pending_shadow_entries():
    checkpoints = [
        {"checkpoint_id": "64a7d4c812988756485531f299aba5bc7f2af23b", "message": "live shadow, not committed"},
        {"checkpoint_id": "01M1TJNMKW7CKJ4NJ8BY6VCQ6B", "agent": "Claude Code", "is_logs_only": True, "message": "Pivot to Warden"},
    ]

    def fake_subprocess_run(cmd, **kwargs):
        if cmd[:3] == ["entire", "checkpoint", "list"]:
            return _fake_run(stdout=json.dumps(checkpoints))
        if cmd[:3] == ["entire", "checkpoint", "explain"]:
            assert cmd[3] == "01M1TJNMKW7CKJ4NJ8BY6VCQ6B", "must use the committed checkpoint, not the pending one"
            return _fake_run(stdout="## Intent\nPivot to Warden")
        raise AssertionError(f"unexpected command {cmd}")

    with patch("subprocess.run", side_effect=fake_subprocess_run):
        cp_id, intent = get_latest_checkpoint()

    assert cp_id == "01M1TJNMKW7CKJ4NJ8BY6VCQ6B"
    assert "Pivot to Warden" in intent


def test_get_latest_checkpoint_degrades_gracefully_when_entire_unavailable():
    with patch("subprocess.run", side_effect=FileNotFoundError("entire: command not found")):
        cp_id, intent = get_latest_checkpoint()
    assert cp_id is None
    assert intent is None


def test_get_latest_checkpoint_degrades_gracefully_on_malformed_json():
    with patch("subprocess.run", return_value=_fake_run(stdout="not json")):
        cp_id, intent = get_latest_checkpoint()
    assert cp_id is None
    assert intent is None


def test_graph_impact_never_asserts_unavailable_output_as_fact():
    with patch("subprocess.run", return_value=_fake_run(returncode=1, stderr="timed out")):
        result = graph_impact("demo_users")
    assert "unavailable" in result
    assert "timed out" in result


def test_graph_impact_returns_raw_output_on_success():
    with patch("subprocess.run", return_value=_fake_run(stdout="  callers: none  \n")):
        result = graph_impact("demo_users")
    assert result == "callers: none"


def test_run_entire_never_raises_on_timeout():
    with patch("subprocess.run", side_effect=subprocess.TimeoutExpired(cmd="entire", timeout=30)):
        out, err = run_entire(["graph", "impact", "--symbol", "x"])
    assert out is None
    assert "30" in err or "Timeout" in err or "timed out" in err.lower()
